N.name: N at this height
N.text: The number of elements in the table a miner must keep in memory. N × 32 bytes ≈ {{gib}} GiB (a theoretical figure — mining software may lay the table out a little differently).

intro: Like Bitcoin, Ergo uses Proof-of-Work: to add a block, a miner has to find a number (a nonce) that makes the hash of the header smaller than a threshold called the target. The difference lies in the function being hashed. Bitcoin uses double SHA-256 — extremely fast, and therefore dominated by specialized ASIC machines. Ergo uses Autolykos, a memory-hard algorithm: mining speed is limited by memory bandwidth, something ordinary GPUs are already very good at.

idea.title: The idea: the k-sum problem
idea.p1: Picture a giant lookup table that only fits in a graphics card's memory. Each mining attempt is “pick 32 random cells from the table, add them up, hash the sum, and check whether you got lucky”. The hard part is not the maths — it is fetching 32 cells from a multi-gigabyte table, billions of times.
idea.p2: Autolykos is based on the k-sum problem: pick k elements from a large list so that their sum satisfies some condition. Concretely, in v2, with k = {{k}}:
idea.li1: There is a table of N elements, each generated by hashing its index together with the block height. The miner precomputes the whole table for the current height and keeps it in the GPU's VRAM.
idea.li2: For each nonce tried, hash (header message ‖ nonce) to derive {{k}} pseudo-random indexes into the table.
idea.li3: Fetch the {{k}} elements at those indexes, add them up, then hash the sum with blake2b256.
idea.li4: If the result (read as an integer) is below the target → block found. Otherwise → change the nonce and try again.
idea.p3: Every attempt needs {{k}} random reads from a table that is gigabytes in size. Recomputing table elements each time instead of storing them is far slower, so whoever has the most memory bandwidth mines fastest. An ASIC that wants to compete also has to carry a large amount of fast memory — at which point it has essentially become a GPU.
idea.figAlt: One Autolykos mining attempt as a loop. The header message plus a nonce are hashed; the hash fans out into 32 random indexes pointing at scattered cells of a large grid, the table of N elements held in a graphics card's VRAM, several GB in size. The 32 picked elements are added together, the sum is hashed with blake2b256, and the result is compared with the target. If it is below the target, a block is found; if not, a red arrow loops back: nonce + 1, try again.
idea.figCaption: Every attempt is {{k}} random reads from a multi-gigabyte table. Memory bandwidth, not raw arithmetic, decides how fast you can go round this loop.

table.title: An ever-growing table N
table.p1: To keep commodity hardware competitive in the long run, the table size N grows over time: it starts at 2<sup>26</sup> (≈ 67 million elements), then from height {{start}} it grows by 5% every {{period}} blocks (~71 days), and stops growing around height {{freeze}}.

versions.title: Autolykos v1 and v2
versions.p1: The first version (v1, used since mainnet launched in 2019) was designed to be non-outsourceable: a solution was tied to the miner's secret key, to make pool mining risky — if a pool handed out work, a miner could simply keep the reward. In practice it didn't stop pools either: the Ergo researchers themselves showed that pools could get around it with collateralized smart contracts. It only made everything more complicated.
versions.p2: The hard fork at block {{height}} (February 2021) introduced Autolykos v2: it dropped non-outsourceability so that mining pools work normally, and introduced the growing-N mechanism described above. The API still shows the four solution fields pk, w, n, d as in v1, but a v2 header only stores pk and n:
versions.pk: pk is still the public key of the miner (or pool) — whoever receives the reward.
versions.w: w is always the secp256k1 generator point G (0279be667e…) — a placeholder constant.
versions.n: n — the 8-byte nonce — is the only part that actually carries information about the solution.

verify.title: Cheap to verify, expensive to find
verify.text: Finding a nonce takes tens of trillions of attempts across the whole network (at ~0.5 TH/s, about 60 trillion per 2-minute block). But to check it, a node only needs to recompute {{k}} table elements at {{k}} indexes — it doesn't need the whole table. That's why a node running on an ordinary computer can still validate every block.
